Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

popular adjective

liked by many

also popularity, well liked, popular with, in favour, a popular place, enjoy popularity among, be popular with

classical

Cic. Off. 3.58: apud omnēs ōrdinēs grātiōsus (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 156, 363: popular, grātiōsus; to be popular with someone, grātiōsus esse apud aliquem

grātiōsus, grātiōsa, grātiōsum

adjective; popular with someone, grātiōsus apud aliquem · Declension on Wiktionary

popular, well liked, in favour (of a person)

A favourite word of Cicero’s, used mostly of persons (Lewis & Short). Popularity is grātia (Traupman 156).

Other words

  • populāris, populāre — popular, pleasing to the people

    adjective, third declension · classical · Cic. Lig. 37: nihil est tam populāre quam bonitās; Cic. Agr. 2.9: quid enim est tam populāre quam pāx? · Declension on Wiktionary

    Of things and measures that please the public. Of a politician, populāris is one who courts the crowd: Cicero glosses it assentātor, a flatterer (Lael. 95). As a noun it is a fellow countryman.

  • acceptus, accepta, acceptum — welcome, popular (with someone: dative)

    adjective (participle of accipiō) · also used · classical · Caes. BG 1.3: maximē plēbī acceptus erat · Declension on Wiktionary

  • favōrābilis, favōrābile — in favour, popular

    adjective, third declension · also used · classical · Vell. 2.34.2 (Lewis & Short); Quint. 12.10.74 (Lewis & Short) · Declension on Wiktionary

    Not before Augustus; perhaps first in Vell. 2.34 (Lewis & Short).

  • celeber, celebris, celebre — of a place: much frequented, busy, popular

    adjective, third declension · also used · classical · Cic. Imp. Pomp. 33: portus celeberrimus (Lewis & Short); Cic. Verr. 2.3.133: in forō celeberrimō (Lewis & Short) · Declension on Wiktionary

  • vulgō — commonly, generally (as most people say or think)

    adverb · also used · classical · Gell. 16.5.1: vocābula quibus vulgō ūtimur · Wiktionary

    For “popular” in the sense “of people in general”: a popular belief is one held by most people, vulgō.

  • grātiam habēre apud — to enjoy popularity among

    avoid · modern · Traupman 156

    Grātiam habēre classically means “to be grateful, to thank” (Ter. Eun. 5.8.61, Lewis & Short s.v. grātia). For “be popular with someone” say grātiōsus esse apud aliquem, which Traupman also gives.

Examples

  • nihil est tam populāre quam bonitās

    nothing is so popular as kindnessCic. Lig. 37

  • quantō plūs propinquōrum, quantō major adfīnium numerus, tantō grātiōsior senectūs

    the more kinsfolk and the greater the number of in-laws, the more cherished is old ageTac. Germ. 20.5

  • grātiōsus est apud omnēs

    he is popular with everyoneTraupman 156

  • grātiōsum (-am) esse apud aliquem

    to be popular with someoneTraupman 363

See also social, people.
